summary: Explains when and how the RSVP extensions for LSP tunnels in RFC 3209 should be used. It covers the principles of operation, deployment guidelines, and known limitations. It is informational.

eli5.summary: This is a guide that says what a special tool is good for, how to use it, and where it falls short, so people can decide whether to use it.

questions: when to use rsvp lsp tunnels
what are the limitations of rsvp te
subtitle: When RSVP-TE is the right tool for setting up explicit MPLS paths, how to deploy it, and where it falls short.

tldr.problem: Operators needed an open, standards-based signaling protocol so label switching routers from different vendors could interoperate for MPLS traffic engineering.
tldr.mechanism: This applicability statement explains where the RSVP extensions for LSP tunnels (RSVP-TE) fit, summarizes how they extend RSVP, gives deployment guidance, and lists limitations.
tldr.outcome: It says RSVP-TE suits explicit LSPs for traffic engineering and measurement, while allowing other protocols. It supports unicast, unidirectional tunnels only.

today: RFC 3210 is an Informational RFC. The unit metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
Service providers wanted traffic engineering in IP networks, built on Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS). That needs a common signaling and label distribution protocol that is open and non-proprietary. The IETF MPLS working group developed the RSVP-TE specification, RFC 3209, to meet this need. It contains the objects, packet formats and procedures to establish and maintain explicit label switched paths (LSPs).

This memo accompanies the submission of that specification to the standards track. It covers only RSVP used to set up unicast LSP-tunnels. It does not prevent other protocols: CR-LDP and RSVP-TE perform similar functions, there is no consensus on which is technically superior, and administrators should choose based on their needs.
sections.eli5: Network owners wanted one common way to lay out special routes. This guide says what the way is for and that other ways are allowed too.

sections.title: What RSVP-TE Adds to RSVP
sections.content:
RSVP-TE adds these functions in an MPLS domain: downstream-on-demand label distribution, explicit LSPs, resource allocation such as bandwidth, smooth rerouting using make-before-break, route tracking, diagnostics, nodal abstraction, and administratively controlled preemption. It adds the LABEL-REQUEST, RECORD-ROUTE, LABEL and EXPLICIT-ROUTE objects and new SESSION objects. All are optional except LABEL-REQUEST and LABEL, which are mandatory to establish LSP-tunnels.

Two things set it apart from original RSVP. First, it is for label switching routers as well as hosts, to set up tunnels and reserve resources for them, whereas RSVP was for hosts reserving resources for micro-flows. Second, a session is implicitly the set of packets assigned the same MPLS label at the tunnel's start. Because traffic is aggregated, the number of sessions does not grow in proportion to the number of flows. This addresses a scaling problem of original RSVP.
sections.eli5: Plain RSVP reserved a lane for one small stream of cars. RSVP-TE reserves one lane for a whole group of cars, so far fewer lanes need tracking.

sections.title: Where It Applies
sections.content:
RSVP-TE is appropriate where explicit LSPs are useful in an MPLS network. They may be set up for measurement, for routing control, or for other administrative reasons. For measurement, a tunnel can carry packet and byte counters, even without bandwidth allocation. For routing control, tunnels can steer subsets of traffic away from the paths chosen by conventional IGP shortest path first computation, for example away from congested resources, and support load balancing.

An optional constraint-based routing entity can compute explicit routes, and IGP advertisements can be extended to carry topology state. These additions are useful but not mandatory. The RFC says RSVP-TE is applicable to traffic engineering in service provider networks and, in some contexts, as a part of an MPLS-based VPN provisioning framework.
sections.eli5: The tool helps count the cars between two spots and steer some of them onto emptier roads when the main road is jammed.

sections.title: Deployment and Policy Guidance
sections.content:
Deployments should have well-defined administrative policies for choosing the nodes that act as tunnel endpoints. A large number of tunnels gives finer control over traffic, but adds operational complexity. In large networks the RFC suggests starting with a simple tunnel topology and adding complexity as traffic patterns are observed or anticipated.

Policies may also guide how much bandwidth, if any, is given to each tunnel, possibly using empirical traffic statistics from the operational network.
sections.eli5: Start with a few routes and add more only when you see you need them. Too many routes make things hard to manage.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content:
The specification supports only unicast LSP-tunnels, so multicast tunnels are not supported. It supports only unidirectional tunnels, so bidirectional ones are not supported.

RSVP's soft state remains a concern, because refresh messages must be sent periodically to keep established tunnels alive. The RFC points to proposals that address this, including the RSVP refresh overhead reduction extensions in RFC 2961.
sections.eli5: It only builds one-way roads for one traveler at a time, and it must keep saying hello to keep the road open.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The memo says it introduces no new security issues. RSVP-TE adds new opaque objects to RSVP, so the security considerations of original RSVP remain relevant. In service provider networks it is mandatory to make sure that only authorized entities can start establishing LSP-tunnels.
sections.eli5: Only people who are allowed should be able to ask for a new road.
